---
title: "Geographical effects across England"
subtitle: "How much of a school's results depends on where it is, once Value Added v2.1 has allowed for its intake; which places stand out; and what we know about why."
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "site_helpers.R"))
G <- readRDS(here::here("data", "geography.rds"))
O <- readRDS(here::here("data", "oac_neighbourhoods.rds"))
B <- readRDS(here::here("data", "bh_effect.rds"))
NC <- tryCatch(readRDS(here::here("data", "neighbourhood_covariates.rds")), error = function(e) NULL)
lv <- function(g, l) G$levels$pct[G$levels$group == g & G$levels$level == l]
rg <- function(g, r) G$reg$pct[G$reg$group == g & G$reg$gor_name == r]
lcor <- function(g, code) O$la_cor$r_w[O$la_cor$group == g & O$la_cor$code == code]
la_g <- function(g) G$la |> filter(group == g)
bh <- function(g, col) G$la[[col]][G$la$group == g & G$la$LANAME == "Brighton and Hove"]
p1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", x)
spread <- function(g) { x <- la_g(g)$pct; diff(quantile(x, c(0.1, 0.9))) }
ac <- function(g, o) G$abs_cor$r[G$abs_cor$group == g & G$abs_cor$outcome == o]
```

::: {.callout-important}
## In short

- **Place matters, but less than the school.** Once v2.1 has allowed for
  intake, a local authority one standard deviation above average adds about
  `r p1(lv("all", "Local authority"))` to its schools' Attainment 8, and a
  region about `r p1(lv("all", "Region"))`. A school's own lasting effect is
  about `r p1(lv("all", "School (lasting)"))`.
- **Place matters most for disadvantaged pupils.** For them the authority
  effect is `r p1(lv("disadvantaged", "Local authority"))` and the region
  effect `r p1(lv("disadvantaged", "Region"))`, against
  `r p1(lv("non_disadvantaged", "Local authority"))` and
  `r p1(lv("non_disadvantaged", "Region"))` for non-disadvantaged pupils.
  Disadvantaged pupils in London do
  `r p1(rg("disadvantaged", "London"))` better than similar pupils
  across England; in the South East, `r p1(abs(rg("disadvantaged", "South East")))`
  worse. London's non-disadvantaged pupils do
  `r p1(abs(rg("non_disadvantaged", "London")))` worse.
- **What goes with it is partly the kind of place, partly the pupils.**
  Disadvantaged pupils do better where schools serve multicultural, urban
  neighbourhoods. They do worse in small-town, coastal and former
  industrial areas ([Neighbourhood types](neighbourhood_types.qmd)).
  Much of that is who the pupils are, since v2.1 has no pupil ethnicity.
  Some is deprivation that the qualification term misses
  ([Neighbourhood covariates](neighbourhood_covariates.qmd)). Most of the
  authority effects remain unexplained.
:::

## How much is place? {#sec-size}

Value Added v2.1 fits each school's results with random effects for its
region and its local authority. These pick up what places have in common
once intake is allowed for. Their size, against each school's own lasting
effect:

```{r}
#| label: fig-levels
#| fig-cap: "How much Attainment 8 varies, once v2.1 has allowed for intake: one standard deviation of the region, local authority and school (lasting) effects, as % of Attainment 8, by group of pupils."
#| fig-height: 3.4
LV_COL <- c("Region" = GREY, "Local authority" = BLUE, "School (lasting)" = DPURPLE)
lvd <- G$levels |> mutate(level = factor(level, names(LV_COL)),
                          grp = factor(GROUP_LABELS[group], rev(GROUP_LABELS)))
ggplot(lvd, aes(pct, grp, fill = level)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", pct)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.1, colour = INK) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = LV_COL, name = NULL, breaks = names(LV_COL)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12)), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "One standard deviation, % of Attainment 8", y = NULL) + theme_note() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

Between the authorities a tenth of the way from the top and a tenth of
the way from the bottom, the gap is about `r p1(spread("all"))` of
Attainment 8 for all pupils (about `r round(spread("all") * 0.475, 1)`
points at the national average), `r p1(spread("disadvantaged"))` for
disadvantaged pupils and `r p1(spread("non_disadvantaged"))` for
non-disadvantaged pupils. That is the difference a place makes to otherwise
similar schools.

This is why Value Added v2.1 is published two ways. **Against England**
keeps the place in: a school in an authority where similar schools do
well looks better. **Within the authority** takes it out, and compares a
school with similar schools nearby.

## The map {#sec-map}

Each authority is coloured by its effect in Value Added v2.1: how far its
schools' results sit from what their intake predicts, as a percentage of
Attainment 8, net of its region.
**[Green]{style="color:#1b7837"} is above what intake predicts (a positive
effect); [purple]{style="color:#762a83"} is below (a negative effect).**
Pale areas are close to zero. These are the same colours as the
[explorer](explore.qmd). Hover over an authority for its figure, interval
and rank.

```{r}
#| include: false
MAP_COL <- c("#762a83", "#af8dc3", "#f7f7f7", "#7fbf7b", "#1b7837")   # below ... above, as the explorer
mk_map <- function(g) {
  d <- G$bounds |> left_join(la_g(g) |> select(LANAME, pct, lo_pct, hi_pct, rank, n_la), by = "LANAME")
  pal <- leaflet::colorNumeric(MAP_COL, domain = c(-8, 8), na.color = "#e8e6ee")
  lab <- sprintf("<b>%s</b><br>%s%% %s<br>95%% interval %s to %s<br>rank %s of %s", d$LANAME,
                 ifelse(is.na(d$pct), "–", sprintf("%+.1f", d$pct)),
                 ifelse(is.na(d$pct), "", ifelse(d$pct >= 0, "above what intake predicts", "below what intake predicts")),
                 sprintf("%+.1f", d$lo_pct), sprintf("%+.1f", d$hi_pct), d$rank, d$n_la)
  leaflet::leaflet(d, height = 560, options = leaflet::leafletOptions(scrollWheelZoom = FALSE)) |>
    leaflet::addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas") |>
    leaflet::addPolygons(fillColor = ~ pal(pmax(pmin(pct, 8), -8)), fillOpacity = 0.85, color = "#ffffff", weight = 0.6,
                         label = lapply(lab, htmltools::HTML),
                         highlightOptions = leaflet::highlightOptions(weight = 2, color = INK, bringToFront = TRUE)) |>
    leaflet::addLegend("topright", colors = rev(MAP_COL),
                       labels = c("+8% or more: above", "+4%", "0: as intake predicts", "−4%", "−8% or less: below"),
                       title = "Against what intake predicts", opacity = 0.9)
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### All pupils

```{r}
mk_map("all")
```

### Disadvantaged pupils

```{r}
mk_map("disadvantaged")
```

### Non-disadvantaged pupils

```{r}
mk_map("non_disadvantaged")
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-regions
#| fig-cap: "Average value added against England by region (schools' average log residual, weighted by years, as %): all, disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils. This includes the region's and its authorities' effects."
#| fig-height: 4.6
rgd <- G$reg |> filter(group %in% c("all", "disadvantaged", "non_disadvantaged")) |>
  mutate(grp = factor(unname(GROUP_LABELS[group]), rev(unname(GROUP_LABELS[c("all", "disadvantaged", "non_disadvantaged")]))))
rord <- rgd |> filter(group == "disadvantaged") |> arrange(pct) |> pull(gor_name)
ggplot(rgd |> mutate(gor_name = factor(gor_name, rord)), aes(pct, gor_name, fill = grp)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = GREY) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = GROUP_COL, name = NULL,
                    breaks = unname(GROUP_LABELS[c("all", "disadvantaged", "non_disadvantaged")])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-6, 6, 2), labels = function(x) ifelse(x == 0, "0%", paste0(sprintf("%+.0f", x), "%"))) +
  labs(x = "Value added against England, % of Attainment 8", y = NULL) + theme_note() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

The regional pattern is different for disadvantaged pupils. For all
pupils, the South West and North East do best, the North West worst.
Non-disadvantaged pupils are similar, with the North East first.
For disadvantaged pupils, London leads at `r sprintf("%+.1f", rg("disadvantaged", "London"))`%,
and the South East is last at `r sprintf("%+.1f", rg("disadvantaged", "South East"))`%.
London's lead belongs to its disadvantaged pupils alone: its non-disadvantaged
pupils are at `r sprintf("%+.1f", rg("non_disadvantaged", "London"))`%.
Brighton and Hove's effect is among the largest in England:
`r sprintf("%+.1f", bh("all", "pct"))`% for all pupils
(`r ord(bh("all", "rank"))` of `r bh("all", "n_la")`),
`r sprintf("%+.1f", bh("disadvantaged", "pct"))`% for disadvantaged pupils
(`r ord(bh("disadvantaged", "rank"))` of `r bh("disadvantaged", "n_la")`) and
`r sprintf("%+.1f", bh("non_disadvantaged", "pct"))`% for non-disadvantaged pupils
(`r ord(bh("non_disadvantaged", "rank"))` of `r bh("non_disadvantaged", "n_la")`).
Its own page examines it.

## What goes with place {#sec-why}

What the evidence on this site says about why places differ:

- **The kind of neighbourhood.** The [Output Area
  Classification](neighbourhood_types.qmd) adds nothing to results within
  an authority. Between authorities it describes the pattern for
  disadvantaged pupils. They do better where schools serve multicultural
  neighbourhoods: group 4c, Challenged Multicultural Communities, has a
  correlation of `r sprintf("%+.2f", lcor("disadvantaged", "4c"))` with
  the authority effect. They do worse among the classification's
  "Baseline UK" neighbourhoods (`r sprintf("%+.2f", lcor("disadvantaged", "6"))`)
  and among small-town (`r sprintf("%+.2f", lcor("disadvantaged", "2a"))`)
  and coastal and former industrial ones (`r sprintf("%+.2f", lcor("disadvantaged", "6b"))`).
  This is the pattern behind London's lead and the South East's position
  for disadvantaged pupils. For non-disadvantaged pupils the same
  correlations are much weaker (4c `r sprintf("%+.2f", lcor("non_disadvantaged", "4c"))`,
  6b `r sprintf("%+.2f", lcor("non_disadvantaged", "6b"))`).
- **Not adult qualifications.** v2.1 already allows for neighbourhood
  education, and the place pattern survives it. Two places with the same
  share of graduates can differ in diversity, migration and the character
  of their towns.
- **Not absence, much.** Absence is in the model, and authorities' absence
  effects barely track their value added effects: no correlation reaches
  0.2 for any of the three groups. For all pupils the largest link is with
  illness absence, `r sprintf("%+.2f", ac("all", "illness"))`: where pupils
  are recorded ill more often than intake predicts, value added is slightly
  higher. It is the same for disadvantaged pupils
  (`r sprintf("%+.2f", ac("disadvantaged", "illness"))`) but not for
  non-disadvantaged pupils (`r sprintf("%+.2f", ac("non_disadvantaged", "illness"))`).
  Brighton and Hove is the clearest case (see
  [What goes with school absence](absence_causes.qmd#sec-place)).
- **A worked example.** [Brighton and Hove](bh_effect.qmd) tests the
  explanations one at a time for one authority.
- **Who the pupils are, and deprivation the qualification term misses.**
  The [neighbourhood covariates experiment](neighbourhood_covariates.qmd)
  added ten Census measures, and each school's own share of White British
  pupils, to the model. For disadvantaged pupils, the school's composition
  and neighbourhood deprivation together take about a fifth off the
  authority effects and over a third off the regional ones. The ethnic
  pattern is mostly the pupils themselves, not the place. For all and
  non-disadvantaged pupils, authority effects move much less.

## How far from school? {#sec-distance}

Where schools are is part of geography too. Across England, children in deprived neighbourhoods usually live closer to a secondary school. In Brighton and Hove they live about a third further away than their neighbours, and absence goes with distance, more for disadvantaged pupils. [Distance to school](distance.qmd) sets out a first test in straight lines.

## What it means {#sec-means}

- **Read value added against England with the place in mind.** Part of a
  school's figure is where it is: up to a few per cent for all and
  non-disadvantaged pupils, more for disadvantaged pupils. The within-authority figure takes that out.
- **Place effects are largest for the pupils policy most wants to help.**
  A disadvantaged pupil's results depend more on the authority and region
  than a non-disadvantaged pupil's do, even with the same intake.
- **Part of the place effect is the pupils.** v2.1 has no measure of
  pupils' ethnicity. The experiment suggests that is much of what makes
  disadvantaged pupils' results look like a place effect. The rest of
  the authority effects are not in the Census at all.

Built by `R/12_geography.R` from the v2.1 model (`R/02_fit_va.R`), with
boundaries from ONS (counties and unitary authorities, December 2023).
